chapter.name: Banks and the Magic of Finance

questions.q: Which description matches a bank as this chapter defines it?
questions.a: It collects money as deposits and lends money to borrowers as loans
o: It collects money as deposits and lends money to borrowers as loans
It prints banknotes and fixes the benchmark interest rate for the country
It is a marketplace where shares of companies are bought and sold
It is a post office scheme that reaches people in remote places

questions.q: Which account has generally no limit on how many times money can be deposited or withdrawn, but earns no interest?
questions.a: Current account
o: Current account
Savings account
Fixed deposit account
Kisan Vikas Patra account

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a part of financial infrastructure as the chapter describes it?
questions.a: A national highway joining two cities
o: A national highway joining two cities
A payment system such as UPI used for transfers
The stock market where shares are traded
A bank that holds the deposits of its customers

questions.q: A fixed deposit differs from a savings account mainly because
questions.a: the money is placed once and kept for a fixed period such as 3 or 5 years
o: the money is placed once and kept for a fixed period such as 3 or 5 years
it is meant only for businesses and traders who make many payments each day
it can be withdrawn from freely with no wait and no limit at all
it never earns interest, as it is a one-time deposit

questions.q: Meghna owns a stationery wholesale shop in Hyderabad. She receives payments from schools and pays suppliers many times every day. Which account suits her shop best?
questions.a: A current account, as it has generally no limit on deposits and withdrawals
o: A current account, as it has generally no limit on deposits and withdrawals
A savings account, as it is meant for traders who pay their suppliers daily and often
A fixed deposit, as it lets her pay suppliers at any time of the day
A savings account, as it places no limit on withdrawals each month

questions.q: Harpreet's grandmother receives a lump sum on retirement that she will not need for 5 years. She wants the bank to return it with interest higher than a savings account gives. Which account should she choose?
questions.a: A fixed deposit account
o: A fixed deposit account
A current account meant for traders
A savings account with limits
A loan account at the bank

questions.q:
Read the statements.
1. A person who opens a bank account is called an account holder.
2. A savings account never places any limit on how often money can be withdrawn.
3. A bank both keeps deposits safe and lends money to others, paying depositors interest.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 are from the chapter. 2 is false: a savings account allows money to be withdrawn, but there are limits on how often each month.
o: 1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A current account earns no interest.
Reason (R): A current account is meant for businesses and traders.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true statements from the chapter, but who the account is meant for does not explain why it earns no interest, so R does not explain A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
(a) What is meant by a deposit?
(b) Describe in one line what a bank does with the deposits it holds.
questions.a: (a) Money placed in a bank account that can be withdrawn as per the terms of the bank and often earns interest. (b) It keeps the money safe and lends it to businesses or other people.
s: Part (a): deposit defined as money placed in a bank account
Part (b): the bank lends deposits to others while keeping them safe

questions.q:
Navdeep deposits ₹3000 every month and takes nothing out.
(a) How much has he put into a savings account in 8 months?
(b) Why will the balance shown in his passbook be more than this figure?
questions.a: (a) 8 x 3000 = ₹24,000. (b) The bank pays interest on the savings, so interest is added to his balance.
s: Part (b): interest paid by the bank is added

questions.q: Differentiate between a savings account and a current account on any two points.
questions.a: A savings account is for individuals, earns interest, and has limits on how often money can be withdrawn each month. A current account is for businesses and traders, earns no interest and generally has no limit on deposits or withdrawals.
s: Two contrasting points on who the accounts are for and interest
A contrast on limits of transactions

questions.q: Name any two services of a bank that the chapter lists when it says banks make monetary transactions easy.
questions.a: Any two of saving money, withdrawing money and borrowing money.
s: First service named
Second service named

questions.q: What is financial infrastructure? Name any two of the parts that make it up.
questions.a: It is a network of banks, payment systems, stock markets and other financial institutions that help people, businesses and the government carry out transactions and manage money. Any two parts, e.g. banks and stock markets.
s: Definition as a network that helps money transactions
Two parts named from banks, payment systems, stock markets, other institutions

questions.q: Sneha says, 'Both a fixed deposit and a savings account pay interest, so a college student who takes out pocket money every week can put all her money in a fixed deposit, which pays more.' Evaluate her claim.
questions.a: She is not right. It is true that both pay interest, but a fixed deposit is a one-time deposit kept for a fixed period of 3 or 5 years, so the student cannot take money out every week. A savings account allows withdrawals, though with limits on how often each month, and suits regular small needs.
s: Verdict that the claim is not right although both earn interest
Fixed deposit is a one-time deposit for a fixed period
Savings account allows withdrawals, with limits each month, so it suits weekly needs

questions.q: Using Navdeep and Rima as your example, explain how a bank links a person who has extra money with a person who needs money.
questions.a: Navdeep deposits his surplus ₹3000 a month in the bank because cash at home is not safe. Rima, who runs a bamboo business, needs money and takes a loan from the bank. The bank uses the money people deposit to lend to borrowers like Rima, and repays depositors with interest.
s: Navdeep's deposit and its reason
Rima's loan for her business
Bank as the link between them, giving interest to depositors

questions.q: Write a short story of three or four lines in which a fixed deposit is the right choice for a family. Mention the amount, the period and what the bank returns at the end.
questions.a: Any suitable story, e.g. the Rao family keeps ₹50,000 for 3 years for a daughter's admission; the bank returns the original ₹50,000 plus interest after 3 years, and the interest is usually higher than a savings account gives.
s: A realistic situation where money is not needed for a fixed period
Bank returns the original amount plus interest
Notes that the interest is usually higher than in a savings account

questions.q: Compare the savings account, the current account and the fixed deposit account on who each is for, the interest earned and how money is withdrawn. Then say which one you would advise a Class 12 student who receives a scholarship of ₹2000 every month and takes out a little at a time, and why.
questions.a: Savings: for individuals who save regularly, earns interest, withdrawals limited each month. Current: for businesses and traders, no interest, generally no limit on transactions. Fixed deposit: one-time deposit for a fixed period like 3 or 5 years, interest usually higher than a savings account, returned with interest at the end. The student saves regularly and withdraws small sums, so a savings account suits her.
s: Savings account: who it is for, interest, withdrawal limits
Current account: who it is for, no interest, no limit
Fixed deposit: one-time, fixed period, higher interest
Recommends the savings account for the student
Reason tied to regular saving and small withdrawals

questions.q: 'Financial infrastructure is as important for a nation's progress as physical infrastructure.' Justify this statement using the chapter.
questions.a: Financial infrastructure is a network of banks, payment systems, stock markets and other institutions. The roads, railways and telecommunication are physical infrastructure, and their development and maintenance have to be funded; financial institutions help raise and move that money. Banks promote savings and give credit, as with Navdeep's deposit and Rima's loan. Together these promote savings, credit and investment, which boosts economic activity and contributes to the nation's prosperity.
s: Defines financial infrastructure with its parts
Links it to funding physical infrastructure
Uses the deposit and loan example
Savings, credit and investment boost economic activity
Concludes about the nation's prosperity

questions.q:
The Eco Club of a Pune school earns money at its monthly Sunday stall. It pays stall rent, seed packets and printing bills several times in a week. The teacher in charge also holds ₹60,000 from a school award. The money will not be needed for the next 18 months, but the school may want it back for a greenhouse after that, perhaps within 3 years. The bank manager says the Club may open any one of the accounts the chapter describes.
(a) Name the type of account the Club should use for the stall payments and give the feature that makes it suit.
(b) Name the type of account that would usually pay the highest interest on the ₹60,000 if left for the full period.
(c) The treasurer suggests the ₹60,000 be kept in the stall account so it is handy. State one thing the school gives up by this.
(d) The greenhouse money may be needed after only 18 months. Choose between a fixed deposit and a savings account for the ₹60,000, and justify with a feature of your choice.
questions.a: (a) A current account: generally no limit on how many times money is deposited or withdrawn. (b) A fixed deposit, as its interest is usually higher than a savings account. (c) It gives up interest, since a current account earns none. (d) Either is acceptable if justified: a fixed deposit for higher interest if the period can be matched to the need, or a savings account if the school may need the money earlier, accepting lower interest and a limit on withdrawals each month.
s: Part (a): current account with its no-limit feature
Part (b): fixed deposit named as the higher-interest type
Part (c): loses the interest
Part (d): picks one and justifies with an account feature

questions.q:
In one week a bank branch near a Delhi market opened 60 new accounts. Of these, 34 were opened by individuals who wanted to save regularly, 11 by traders who make and receive payments all day, and 15 were one-time deposits that the customers promised to leave untouched for fixed periods.
(a) Name the type of account opened by each of the three groups.
(b) How many of the 60 accounts earn interest for their holders?
(c) Why do traders still open the type that earns no interest?
(d) Mrs Kapoor, a teacher, walks in with ₹80,000. She wants some interest but may need part of the money in an emergency within a year. Which of the two interest-earning types would you advise, and what does she give up?
questions.a: (a) Savings account, current account, fixed deposit. (b) Savings 34 + fixed deposit 15 = 49 accounts; the 11 current accounts earn no interest. (c) Their businesses need generally no limit on how many times money is deposited or withdrawn. (d) Either is acceptable if justified: a savings account gives access in an emergency but with lower interest and a limit on withdrawals each month; a fixed deposit pays usually higher interest but the money is kept for the fixed period, so she gives up easy access.
s: Part (a): three account types matched to groups
Part (c): no limit on transactions needed by businesses
Part (d): a chosen type justified with a feature

questions.q:
Match each term in Column A with its meaning in Column B.
Column A: 1. Deposit  2. Account holder  3. Fixed deposit  4. Current account
Column B: a. a person or business that has opened a bank account  b. money placed in a bank account  c. a one-time deposit kept for a period like 3 or 5 years  d. an account for traders that earns no interest
questions.a: A deposit is money placed in an account; the account holder is the person or business; a fixed deposit is kept for a fixed period; a current account suits traders and earns no interest.

questions.q: In the chapter, what is compounding?
questions.a: Earning interest on the previous interest as well as on the original amount
o: Earning interest on the previous interest as well as on the original amount
Earning the same amount of interest every year on the original deposit alone
Paying back a loan in equal parts along with its interest each year
Doubling the deposit every year by adding the same sum again

In a passbook, money that is taken out of the account is recorded as a
questions.a: debit

credit
deposit of interest
benchmark entry

questions.q: Which statement about the king and the sage's chessboard story is NOT correct?
questions.a: The sage asked for the same number of grains on each of the 64 squares
o: The sage asked for the same number of grains on each of the 64 squares
The eighth square had 128 grains, the last square of the top row of the board
The 16th square had 32,768 grains as the grains kept on doubling each time
By the 32nd square there were over 210 crore grains

questions.q: Dhruv deposits ₹4000 at 10% interest a year and takes nothing out. In his passbook the interest for the second year is more than for the first. Which idea explains this?
questions.a: Year 2 interest is worked out on ₹4400, including the interest earned in year 1
o: Year 2 interest is worked out on ₹4400, including the interest earned in year 1
Year 2 interest is worked out on ₹4000 plus the bank's reserve money
The bank lends his money at a higher rate in year 2 and passes all of that gain on to him
The bank raises his rate from 10% to 11% in year 2 as a reward for staying

questions.q: Rukmini's passbook shows two lines: 'Cash deposited by self ₹4,500' and 'Electricity bill paid ₹1,320'. How are the two lines recorded?
questions.a: The first is a credit and the second is a debit
o: The first is a credit and the second is a debit
The first is a debit and the second is a credit
Both are credits, as cash is involved in each
Both are debits, as both appear in the passbook

questions.q:
Read the statements about ₹1000 deposited at 6% a year.
1. The interest in the second year is again ₹60.
2. Earning interest on previous interest is called compounding.
3. If left for 12 years, the money grows to ₹2012.20.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 are from the chapter. 1 is false: the second year's interest is 6% of ₹1060, that is ₹63.60.
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): On a deposit of ₹1000 at 6%, the interest rises from ₹60 in the first year to ₹63.60 in the second.
Reason (R): In the second year the interest is worked out on ₹1060, not on ₹1000.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: The interest grows because it is calculated on the amount that already includes the first year's interest, so R explains A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Aarav's ₹2000 earns 5% a year.
(a) Find his amount at the end of year 1.
(b) Find the interest for year 2 and say how it compares with the interest for year 1.
questions.a: (a) 2000 + 5% of 2000 = ₹2,100. (b) 5% of 2100 = ₹105, which is ₹5 more than the ₹100 earned in year 1.
s: Part (b): ₹105, which is ₹5 more than year 1

questions.q:
In the sage's story the 11th square had 1024 grains.
(a) How many grains go on the 12th and the 13th squares?
(b) Is the increase from the 12th to the 13th square bigger or smaller than from the 11th to the 12th? Give both figures.
questions.a: (a) 2048 and 4096. (b) The increase from the 11th to the 12th is 1024 and from the 12th to the 13th is 2048, so the later increase is bigger.
s: Part (a): 2048 and 4096
Part (b): increases 1024 and 2048, later one bigger

questions.q: Define 'interest' and 'compounding' in one line each.
questions.a: Interest is the amount charged for borrowing money or the amount gained by lending money, usually a percentage. Compounding is the process of earning interest on previous interest.
s: Interest defined as money gained or charged, as a percentage
Compounding defined as interest on previous interest

questions.q: What is a passbook, and why is it important to keep such records of transactions?
questions.a: A passbook is a diary-like document given by the bank that records all receipts (credits) and payments (debits) in the account and is updated at the bank. Records let the holder track many deposits and withdrawals.
s: Passbook as a record of receipts and payments
Reason: to track many transactions

questions.q:
Kabir deposits money at a fixed rate and withdraws nothing. At the end of year 1 his amount is ₹3,120 and at the end of year 2 it is ₹3,244.80.
(a) Find the interest he earned in year 2.
(b) Find the rate of interest a year, and say on which amount the year 2 interest was worked out.
questions.a: (a) 3,244.80 - 3,120 = ₹124.80. (b) 124.80 / 3,120 x 100 = 4% a year, worked out on ₹3,120, the amount at the end of year 1, not on the original deposit.
s: Part (b): 4% a year on ₹3,120 (year 1 amount)

questions.q: A student says, 'In a bank, ₹1000 at 6% earns ₹60 every year, so after 12 years I will have ₹1,720.' Using the first two years, show that this cannot be right.
questions.a: In year 2 the interest is 6% of ₹1060 = ₹63.60, not ₹60, since interest is earned on the previous interest too. The yearly interest keeps growing, so after 12 years the money is ₹2012.20, which is more than ₹1,720.
s: Year 2 interest ₹63.60, not ₹60
Reason: interest on the previous interest (compounding)

questions.q: Imran says, 'In a bank account compounding doubles the money every year, as the rice doubled on each square.' Do you agree? Use the figures of the chapter.
questions.a: No. The rice doubled on every square in the story, but ₹1000 at 6% became ₹1060 after one year and ₹1,123.60 after two, far from doubling each year. It took 12 years for the amount to reach ₹2012.20. Both show growth on growth, but at very different speeds.
s: Verdict that the claim is wrong
Figures ₹1060 and ₹1,123.60 or ₹2012.20 after 12 years
Distinguishes the doubling in the story from 6% growth

questions.q: A passbook shows exactly ₹2,100 at the end of one year of deposit. Write a short story with an amount deposited and a yearly rate that fit this, and then state the amount at the end of the second year at the same rate.
questions.a: For example, Divya deposits ₹2000 at 5% a year: 2000 + 100 = ₹2,100; year 2 adds 5% of 2100 = ₹105, giving ₹2,205. Another fit: ₹1875 at 12% gives ₹2,100 and then ₹2,352.
s: A realistic story with a deposit and rate
Figures that really give ₹2,100 after a year
Second-year amount worked on ₹2,100

questions.q: Suppose ₹1000 earns 6% a year. Compare the amount after 3 years if interest were paid only on the original ₹1000 with the amount after 3 years under compounding (use ₹1,123.60 for the end of year 2). Round to the nearest paisa and explain why the gap grows.
questions.a: Only on the original: 3 x ₹60 = ₹180, so ₹1,180. Compounding: end of year 2 is ₹1,123.60; year 3 interest 6% of 1123.60 = ₹67.42, giving ₹1,191.02. The gap is ₹11.02. The gap grows because each year's interest is earned on a bigger amount that includes earlier interest.
s: ₹1,180 on the original amount alone
Year 3 interest of about ₹67.42 on ₹1,123.60
Compounded amount ₹1,191.02
Gap of ₹11.02
Reason: interest is earned on previous interest

questions.q: 'Small amounts can grow into large sums over time.' Justify this using both the deposit example and the king and sage story in the chapter.
questions.a: A ₹1000 deposit at 6% earns ₹60 in year 1 and ₹63.60 in year 2 because interest is earned on previous interest; left for 12 years it becomes ₹2012.20. In the story the sage asked for one grain on the first square, doubling each time over 64 squares. The 8th square had 128 grains, the 16th had 32,768 and by the 32nd there were over 210 crore. The king saw how powerful exponential growth is, as small amounts grow into large sums.
s: Deposit example: ₹60 then ₹63.60 and ₹2012.20 after 12 years
Story: one grain doubling, with 128, 32,768 and over 210 crore
Links both to compounding and long periods

questions.q:
Tara and Uma each receive ₹8,000 as a prize and put it in a bank that pays 5% interest a year. Tara leaves everything in the account for 3 years. Uma takes out the year's interest every year to spend and leaves the ₹8,000 untouched. Uma's family needs about ₹400 every year for her school bus pass top-up.
(a) What is Tara's amount at the end of year 1?
(b) How much interest does Tara earn in year 2?
(c) After 3 years, by how much has Tara's money grown, and how much interest in all has Uma collected?
(d) Which plan would you advise Uma, and why?
questions.a: (a) 8000 + 5% of 8000 = ₹8,400. (b) 5% of 8400 = ₹420. (c) Tara: year 3 interest is 5% of 8820 = ₹441, so her amount is ₹9,261 and the growth is ₹1,261; Uma collects 3 x ₹400 = ₹1,200. (d) Either is acceptable if argued: Tara's plan ends with ₹61 more (₹1,261 against ₹1,200) because of interest on interest, but gives no cash on the way; Uma's plan gives the ₹400 each year that her family needs.
s: Part (b): ₹420
Part (c): ₹1,261 growth and ₹1,200 interest
Part (d): chooses a plan with the figures to support it

questions.q:
Roshni's passbook for March opens with a balance of ₹15,000. The lines are: 3 March, salary received ₹28,000; 5 March, house rent paid ₹9,500; 12 March, electricity bill paid ₹1,320; 20 March, tuition fees received ₹6,000; 28 March, groceries paid ₹4,780. Her bank pays 6% interest a year on money left in the account.
(a) Which of the lines are debits?
(b) What are the total credits and total debits for March?
(c) What is her balance at the end of March?
(d) She can spend ₹15,000 on a tablet now or leave it in the account for a year. Find the interest that ₹15,000 would earn in one year and advise her.
questions.a: (a) Rent, electricity and groceries. (b) Credits 28,000 + 6,000 = ₹34,000; debits 9,500 + 1,320 + 4,780 = ₹15,600. (c) 15,000 + 34,000 - 15,600 = ₹33,400. (d) 6% of 15,000 = ₹900 in a year. Either choice is acceptable if justified: waiting earns ₹900 and the balance still covers her needs, while buying now gives the use of the tablet at once.
s: Part (a): three payment lines as debits
Part (b): ₹34,000 credits and ₹15,600 debits
Part (d): ₹900 and a justified advice

questions.q: According to the chapter, a bank earns income because it
questions.a: charges more interest on loans than it pays on deposits

prints the notes that it lends to the borrowers

questions.q:
Read the statements.
1. Banks keep reserve money and do not lend all the deposits as loans.
2. A bank always lends out every rupee that is deposited with it.
3. Under the Jan Dhan Yojana, an account holder must keep a minimum balance and pay fees.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Only 1 is correct. 2 is false because banks keep reserves, and 3 is false because the scheme gives accounts without a minimum balance or fees.
o: 1 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Over 50 crore accounts were opened under the Jan Dhan Yojana, mainly by women.
Reason (R): The scheme required every account holder to maintain a minimum balance.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is from the chapter. R is false: the scheme offered accounts without a minimum balance or fees, which is what made it easy to join.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Ananya deposits ₹1,000 at 4% a year. The bank lends the ₹1,000 to Mohit at 9% a year.
(a) How much does Mohit repay at the end of the year?
(b) How much does Ananya receive, and how much does the bank earn?
s: Part (b): ₹1,040 to Ananya and ₹50 earned

questions.q:
(a) Why do banks charge a higher interest on loans than they pay on deposits?
(b) Why can a bank not lend out every rupee that people deposit?
questions.a: (a) The difference between the two rates is the source of income for the banks. (b) Banks keep reserve money, so they do not lend all the deposits to individuals or businesses.
s: Part (a): the difference in rates is the bank's income
Part (b): banks keep reserve money

questions.q: Name two purposes for which individuals take bank loans and two for which businesses do.
questions.a: Individuals: buying a house or a vehicle, funding education. Businesses: buying new machinery and raw materials, transporting products, launching new products in markets (any two).
s: Two purposes of individuals
Two purposes of businesses

questions.q: Rukmini cooks in a Hyderabad school. Earlier her wages came in cash through a contractor; now they are paid straight into her Jan Dhan account. State two benefits to her that the chapter names for such direct transfers.
questions.a: Direct transfers reduce middlemen, and they ensure timely payment of her wages.
s: Fewer middlemen
Timely payment of the wages

questions.q: What is a loan? State what the borrower must do after the specified period.
questions.a: A loan is an amount borrowed from banks or financial institutions, with the obligation to repay it with interest at a later time. After the specified period the borrower repays the loan amount along with the interest.
s: Loan defined as money borrowed with an obligation to repay
Repayment of the amount along with interest

questions.q: Dev says, 'A bank lends out every rupee people deposit, so on ₹1,000 of deposits it earns loan interest on the whole ₹1,000.' Do you agree? Use the chapter.
questions.a: No. The chapter says banks have reserve money and do not lend all the deposits as loans to individuals or businesses. So interest on loans is earned only on the part that is lent out, and the bank's income is the difference between the interest it charges on that part and the interest it pays depositors.
s: Verdict that the claim is wrong
Banks keep reserve money and do not lend all deposits
Loan interest is earned only on the lent part; income is the difference in rates

questions.q: A shopkeeper says, 'A bank loan is a help, so after I take ₹50,000 for machinery I will never have to return more than ₹50,000.' Using the chapter, show why this cannot be right.
questions.a: The chapter says that after a specified period the borrower repays the loan amount along with the interest charged by the bank. So the shopkeeper must return more than ₹50,000. This interest is a source of income for the bank, since it charges a higher rate on loans than it pays to depositors, and without it the bank could not pay its depositors.
s: Loan is repaid after a specified period
Interest is repaid along with the loan amount, so more than ₹50,000
Interest on loans is the bank's income and pays depositors

questions.a: Any suitable story, e.g. Salma takes a loan to buy raw materials for her bakery in Kochi. After the agreed period she repays the loan amount along with the interest the bank charges. The interest is higher than what the bank pays depositors, which is how the bank earns.

questions.q:
A cooperative bank branch in Nashik holds a single deposit of ₹1,00,000 from Balu, on which it pays 3% interest a year. It lends ₹60,000 to Fatima's tailoring unit at 8% and ₹30,000 to Gurpreet to buy a vehicle at 9%. The remaining money is kept aside. Fatima has now asked the bank to lower her rate to 5%.
(a) How much interest does the bank pay Balu in a year?
(b) How much interest does it collect from the two borrowers, and how much of the deposit is kept aside?
(c) What is the bank's earning from this deposit, using your answers to (a) and (b)?
(d) If Fatima's rate falls to 5% and nothing else changes, what is the bank's earning? Should the bank agree? Justify.
questions.a: (a) 3% of 1,00,000 = ₹3,000. (b) 4,800 + 2,700 = ₹7,500 collected; 1,00,000 - 60,000 - 30,000 = ₹10,000 kept aside as reserve. (c) 7,500 - 3,000 = ₹4,500. (d) Fatima would pay 3,000, so the collection becomes ₹5,700 and the earning ₹2,700, a fall of ₹1,800. Either decision is acceptable if justified: the cut helps a borrower's business, but the bank's income from the difference between rates falls by 40%.
s: Part (b): ₹7,500 collected and ₹10,000 kept aside
Part (d): ₹2,700 and a justified decision

questions.a: (a) No minimum balance and no fees. (b) 575 - 160 = 415 new account holders; 160 of 640 is 25%. (d) Either is acceptable if justified: direct transfer to the 138 reduces middlemen and ensures timely payment, and the 12 can open accounts without a minimum balance or fees; the agent route reaches all at once but keeps the middleman.
s: Part (a): no minimum balance and no fees
Part (b): 415 new and 25%
Part (c): about 70%, women a majority, fits the chapter
Part (d): a way chosen and justified with a chapter benefit

Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 are from the chapter. 2 is false: a fall in the prices of the shares of many companies together is a stock market crash, and a rise is a boom.
o: 1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A person who buys a share of a company becomes a lender to that company, according to the chapter's definition of a share.
Reason (R): A share is a unit of ownership in a company.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is false: the buyer becomes a part-owner of the company, not a lender. R is a true statement from the chapter.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

questions.q:
The chapter compares a company to a big chapati.
(a) What does each share stand for in this comparison?
(b) What does owning more shares mean for the owner?
questions.a: (a) Each share is one piece of the chapati, that is, a part of the company. (b) The more shares a person owns, the higher her ownership of the company.
s: Part (a): a share as one piece of the company
Part (b): more shares mean higher ownership

questions.q:
In one week the prices of the shares of 40 of the 50 listed companies on an exchange fell sharply together.
(a) What is this situation called?
(b) How is it different from the price of a single company's shares falling after its workers go on strike?
questions.a: (a) A stock market crash. (b) A crash is a fall in the prices of the shares of many companies at the same time, whereas a strike affects only one company's own performance and so only its share price.
s: Part (a): stock market crash
Part (b): many companies together versus one company's own problem

questions.q: Why do companies issue shares, and why do people buy them?
questions.a: Companies issue shares to raise funds for their operations. People buy shares to put their savings where they expect the value to rise when the share price increases.
s: Companies raise funds
Buyers expect the price to increase

questions.q: State two precautions that the chapter advises for staying safe from financial fraud.
questions.a: Never share personal information such as phone number, account number, home address, passwords or OTPs with strangers; avoid clicking unknown links or videos in messages; do not store account passwords or debit card PINs on devices (any two).
s: First precaution
Second precaution

questions.q:
(a) Where does the actual buying and selling of shares take place?
(b) How have share transactions changed since the Bombay Stock Exchange began in 1875?
questions.a: (a) At the stock exchange. (b) They were first done manually using paper tickets and have been replaced by digital transactions using advanced computers and other devices.
s: Part (a): the stock exchange
Part (b): paper tickets replaced by digital transactions

questions.q: Rahul says, 'A share price depends only on how well the company is doing, so a change in the government's tax rules cannot affect it.' Do you agree? Give reasons.
questions.a: No. A company that is doing well makes its shares more valuable and one with a strike or big loss lowers them, but government policy changes such as new laws and tax rules, political instability, wars or economic shocks can also cause price changes.
s: Verdict that the claim is wrong
Company performance as one factor
Tax rules and other outside factors also change prices

questions.q: A friend says, 'Buying shares can never cause a loss, since people buy them expecting the price to rise.' Maya bought 50 shares at ₹120 each; after a workers' strike the price is ₹95 per share. Show that a loss is possible.
questions.a: Maya paid 50 x 120 = ₹6,000. At ₹95 the 50 shares are worth 50 x 95 = ₹4,750. She is down by ₹1,250. The chapter says trading shares can bring gains or losses, and a strike is a problem that lowers a share's price.
s: Cost ₹6,000
Value ₹4,750 and loss of ₹1,250
Link to the chapter's gains or losses and the strike

questions.q: Write a short message that a fraudster might send, and then write the reply or advice you would give to someone who receives it. Mention what to report and where.
questions.a: For example: 'Your KYC is expiring, click this link and send your OTP.' Advice: this asks for an OTP and an unknown link, which fraudsters use to get bank details and download harmful apps; do not click or share it, and report the fraud on helpline 1930 or the National Cybercrime Reporting Portal.
s: A fake message asking for an OTP, details or a link
Identifies why it is a fraud
Do not respond and report on 1930 or the portal

questions.q: Using the restaurant example from the chapter, explain how the stock market helps both a company that needs money and a person who has savings. Why must the saver still be careful?
questions.a: A restaurant owner who wants to expand can take money from friends in exchange for a share of the profits, making them part-owners. Similarly, a share is part-ownership in a company, so a company issues shares to raise funds for its operations. A saver buys shares expecting their value to rise when the share price increases. But share prices rise and fall with the company's performance, policy changes and shocks, so trading can bring gains or losses.
s: Restaurant example: friends become part-owners
Share as part-ownership in a company
Companies raise funds by issuing shares
Savers buy expecting price to rise
Prices fluctuate, so gains or losses are possible

questions.q: 'Digital payments have made life easier, but users must beware of fraud.' Justify this statement using the chapter.
questions.a: UPI gives quick payments from a phone using a QR code or phone number and reduces the need for passbook updates. But fraudsters trick people through fake calls or messages to download harmful apps or share bank details or OTPs, which gives them access to the phone or computer to steal personal data and drain the bank account. To stay safe, never share personal information or OTPs with strangers, avoid unknown links and do not store PINs on devices. Frauds can be reported on helpline 1930 or the National Cybercrime Reporting Portal.
s: Convenience of digital payments
How fraudsters trick people
What they can steal or drain
Safety rules named
Reporting on 1930 or the portal

questions.q:
Gopal bought 100 shares of Kaveri Textiles on Monday. The closing price of one share over the week was: Monday ₹240, Tuesday ₹252, Wednesday ₹258, Thursday ₹219 and Friday ₹201. Gopal does not know why the price fell on Thursday.
(a) What do people believe about a company when its share price rises, as it did from Monday to Wednesday?
(b) By how much did the price of one share fall from Wednesday to Friday?
(c) What is the change in the value of Gopal's 100 shares between Monday and Friday?
(d) Gopal can sell on Friday or wait. Name one reason from the chapter that could explain a fall, then say which you would advise, and why.
questions.a: (a) That the company is doing well and will earn money. (b) 258 - 201 = ₹57. (c) 100 x 240 = ₹24,000 on Monday and 100 x 201 = ₹20,100 on Friday, a fall of ₹3,900. (d) Possible reasons: a problem in the company such as a strike, or outside factors such as policy changes, tax rules, political instability, war or economic shocks. Either decision is acceptable if justified: selling stops further loss, while waiting may recover the price, but the chapter says prices can keep falling.
s: Part (a): a rise reflects belief that the company does well
Part (b): ₹57
Part (c): ₹3,900 fall
Part (d): a reason named and a decision with a justification

questions.q:
The cyber club of a Kochi school asked the parents of 120 students about fraud. Of them 45 had received fake calls or messages: 30 were calls asking for an OTP or bank details and 15 were messages with unknown links. Among the 30 callers' targets, 18 gave away details; among the 15 who got links, 3 clicked on them. The club has room to print one safety rule in very large letters on its poster.
(a) Name two things the chapter says fraudsters trick people into doing, and the helpline the poster should carry.
(b) What percentage of the 120 parents received fake calls or messages?
(c) Compare the percentage who gave away details with the percentage who clicked a link.
(d) Which rule would you print largest, and why?
questions.a: (a) Downloading harmful apps and sharing bank details or OTPs; helpline 1930. (b) 45 of 120 is 37.5%. (c) 18 of 30 is 60% who gave away details, and 3 of 15 is 20% who clicked a link. (d) Either rule is acceptable if justified: 'Never share OTPs or personal information' since 60% fell for it, or 'Avoid unknown links' since a harmful app can give access to the whole phone.
s: Part (a): harmful apps and sharing bank details or OTPs, and helpline 1930
Part (c): 60% against 20%
Part (d): a rule justified with the data
